source.title: Samsone: A Family of Open Small Audio Language Models for On-Device Inference
source.authors: Piotr Masztalski; Michal K. Grzeszczyk; Olaf Sikorski

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream audio-task performance across three sizes of its own audio-language model family, extending scale-related observations to audio models. It does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream benchmark results for Samsone models at three sizes. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Table 2's multi-level columns are not reliably assignable in the flattened text, so its exact scores are not recorded as rows; the paper's textual claims about those benchmarks are summarized in authors_conclusion.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream audio-task scores across three sizes of its own audio-language model family (99M, 134M, 356M). The authors present this as consistent with scaling laws, so it bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. It measures no pretraining loss and fits no curve. The size variants are confounded: 99M is a depth-pruned 134M, and 356M uses a different backbone and learning rate. Fine-tuning data is fixed.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors state that Samsone's performance gain correlates with size increase, consistent with Kaplan et al. [34]. Their main claims concern state-of-the-art results among small audio models and on-device efficiency. They fit no scaling law and make no loss predictions.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains audio-language models on audio question-answering datasets and evaluates downstream audio-task scores across three model sizes; it does not use the original text-language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling and compute-allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size is varied across three Samsone variants; the AudioCaps ACE score does not increase from 134M to 356M.
record.problems: Only three model sizes are compared, with no fitted predictive relationship or uncertainty estimates. The variants differ in backbone size and pruning, so the comparison is not a controlled test of a general scaling law. Table 2's exact benchmark-score mapping is unclear in the flattened text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports MMAU and MMAU-Pro comparisons, but its multi-level columns are flattened such that exact values cannot be assigned reliably to the family models and metrics. Its qualitative claims are noted in gate_note and authors_conclusion.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted relation, no extrapolation, and no link to pretraining loss. There are only three confounded size points, and no data or compute scaling.
All of V1; no held-out pretraining loss is measured.
All of V4. Depth pruning changes the parameter count, so it is not a fixed-size shape comparison.
All of V5; no loss power law is fitted for audio models.

missing.what: MMAU average across sizes, inferred column mapping: test-mini 57.20/63.00/63.70 and test 58.13/61.33/62.00 for 99M/134M/356M.
Per-domain MMAU scores where 356M falls below 134M: sound test-mini 75.98 vs 76.28; speech test-mini 44.74 vs 46.25 and test 45.90 vs 47.90. Music scores rise.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 2 values are recoverable from the flattened text. The column order (sound test-mini, sound test, music test-mini, music test, then speech, averages and MMAU-Pro) is consistent with the large-model block, so the missing entries use this mapping. It should be checked against the PDF. This is a weak test of V6: three sizes, models built by pruning or backbone swap rather than controlled scaling, fixed fine-tuning data, a different learning rate for 356M, and no uncertainty estimates. Per-row states for single size points are not meaningful on their own; each row should take the next-smaller size as its baseline.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token scaling exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper trains audio models, but does not test whether the claimed pretraining-loss power-law form transfers to audio or other regimes.

Reports downstream benchmark scores at three model sizes, but does not fit or validate a predictive relationship, report pretraining-loss correlations, or test other downstream task families beyond the listed audio benchmarks.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, and no analysis of curves bending away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Clotho SPICE, ClothoAQA accuracy, Clotho CLE accuracy, MMAU average and MMAU-Pro across 99M→134M→356M
relationships.reason: Scores are non-decreasing with size: ClothoAQA 71.8/73.8/74.5 (r7-r9), Clotho SPICE 11.1/11.6/11.7 (r4-r6), CLE 92.4/93.4/93.7 (r10-r12). The MMAU average and MMAU-Pro also rise (text Table 2, not in the rows).
relationships.display_finding: ClothoAQA scores increased 71.8→73.8→74.5, SPICE 11.1→11.6→11.7 and CLE 92.4→93.4→93.7, while MMAU average and MMAU-Pro also improved.

relationships.condition: Specific benchmarks and size steps, especially 134M→356M
relationships.reason: Some size steps show no gain: AudioCaps SPICE is flat 99M→134M (r1-r2), and ACE is flat-to-lower 134M→356M (r14-r15). Other 134M→356M gains are tiny (r6, r12). MMAU sound and speech scores drop at 356M (Table 2 text). The size variants are confounded by pruning, backbone and learning rate.
relationships.display_finding: AudioCaps SPICE stayed flat from 99M to 134M, ACE stayed flat or declined from 134M to 356M, and MMAU sound and speech scores fell at 356M, with size comparisons confounded by pruning, backbone and learning rate.
